cards.question: What is variation (magnetic declination)?
options: The angle between true north and magnetic north at a given place
The angle between magnetic north and compass north on a particular heading
The difference between the course steered and the course made good
cards.explanation: Variation is the horizontal angle between true (geographic) north and magnetic north. It depends on location, changes slowly over time, and is printed in the chart's compass rose.

cards.question: What is deviation?
options: The angle between magnetic north and compass north, caused by the vessel's own magnetism
The angle between true north and magnetic north
The sideways push of the boat caused by the wind
cards.explanation: Deviation is the magnetic compass error caused by the boat's own magnetic field (engine, steel, electronics). It changes with the vessel's heading and is listed in a deviation card.

cards.question: Your compass heading is 100°, deviation 2°E and variation 4°E. What is the true heading?
cards.explanation: Easterly errors are added when converting compass to true ('error east, compass least'): 100° + 2° + 4° = 106°.

cards.question: A magnetic bearing is 215° and the variation is 6°W. What is the true bearing?
cards.explanation: When converting magnetic to true, westerly variation is subtracted: 215° − 6° = 209°. (An easterly variation would be added.)

cards.question: You take compass bearings of two charted objects at the same time. What do the two plotted position lines give you?
options: A fix — your position is where the two position lines cross
Only an estimated position, because bearings ignore the tide
The course to steer to the nearest object
cards.explanation: Two (preferably three) simultaneous bearings of charted objects plot as position lines; their intersection is a fix. A good cut has the lines crossing near 90°.

cards.question: Two charted objects are seen exactly in line (a transit). What is this most useful for?
options: A very accurate position line, and a check of the compass error
Measuring the rate of the tidal stream
Finding the depth of water under the keel
cards.explanation: When two objects are in transit (in line) you are on the line joining them — an extremely accurate position line that needs no compass. Comparing its true bearing with the compass bearing also reveals compass error.

cards.question: Only one charted object is visible. How can you still obtain a fix?
options: Take a bearing, run on a known course and distance, then take a second bearing and transfer the first (a running fix)
Take the same bearing twice from the same spot
You cannot — a fix always needs two objects
cards.explanation: A running fix uses one object: a bearing, then after a measured run (course and distance) a second bearing. The first position line is transferred along the run; the transferred line and the second bearing cross at the fix.

cards.question: What is a dead reckoning (DR) position?
options: A position from course steered and distance run only, with no allowance for tide or leeway
A position found from two or more bearings
A position that already includes the effect of tidal stream and leeway
cards.explanation: A DR position uses only course steered and distance run from a known position. Adding the estimated tidal stream (set and drift) and leeway turns it into an estimated position (EP).

cards.question: In tidal calculations, what do 'set' and 'drift' mean?
options: Set is the direction the tidal stream flows towards; drift is its rate (distance over the period)
Set is the stream's speed; drift is the direction it comes from
Set is the leeway angle; drift is the boat's speed through the water
cards.explanation: Set is the direction towards which the tidal stream flows; drift is how far it would carry you over the period. They are applied to the water track to find the ground track.

cards.question: What is leeway?
options: The angle a boat is pushed downwind of its heading by the wind
The difference between true and magnetic north
The distance run through the water in one hour
cards.explanation: Leeway is the sideways, downwind displacement caused by wind. It offsets the water track to the downwind side and must be allowed for when working up an estimated position or a course to steer.

cards.question: At 6 knots, how far do you travel in 90 minutes?
options: 9 nautical miles
6 nautical miles
4 nautical miles
cards.explanation: Distance = speed × time = 6 kn × 1.5 h = 9 NM. A knot is one nautical mile per hour.

cards.question: You cover 12 nautical miles in 2 hours. What is your speed over the ground?
options: 6 knots
12 knots
24 knots
cards.explanation: Speed = distance ÷ time = 12 NM ÷ 2 h = 6 knots.
